summary:
The Isle of Man is a self-legislating Crown Dependency. Its parliament, Tynwald, legislates on these questions itself, and United Kingdom statutes reach the island only by Order in Council rather than automatically.

The Gender Recognition Act 2009 (c.11) allows transgender people to change their legal gender and have the new gender recognised.

The Equality Act 2017, which received royal assent on 18 July 2017 and was largely brought into force on 1 January 2019, lists gender reassignment as a protected characteristic and as a ground on which discrimination is prohibited. A ban on conversion therapy covering sexual orientation and gender identity was passed in 2020 as an amendment to the sexual offences bill in the Legislative Council and took effect in 2024; the Isle of Man was the first part of the British Isles to prohibit the practice.

Partner recognition is established. Civil partnerships became available to same-sex couples under the Civil Partnership Act 2011 (c.2) on 6 April 2011, and same-sex marriage took effect on 22 July 2016 after royal assent on 19 July 2016. A civil partnership converts into a marriage without a second ceremony, and the first conversion was completed within days of entry into force, which indicates routine registration rather than discretionary approval.

Parental recognition is narrower than the marriage position. Full joint and stepchild adoption has been open to same-sex couples since 6 April 2011 and lesbian couples have access to artificial insemination, but as of an August 2023 consultation same-sex couples are not recognised as parents on birth certificates for children born through IVF or surrogacy, and no Manx law acknowledges surrogacy. A trans visitor whose relationship is read as same-sex under local law would meet that gap.

Sexual-conduct law on the island has been gender-neutral since the Sexual Offences (Amendment) Act 2006 (c.3), which set a single age of consent of sixteen for all sexual conduct regardless of gender and sexual orientation.

A hate crime bill that would explicitly include gender reassignment alongside sexual orientation and marital or civil partnership status was put to community consultation in July 2022. The sources reviewed do not record its enactment.
tangentialFactors:
Tynwald Hansard for 26 April 2016 records the Legislative Council's third reading of the Marriage and Civil Partnership (Amendment) Bill 2016 alongside consideration of the Equality Bill 2016, the primary legislative record of the island's marriage reform. Chief Minister Allan Bell had publicly backed same-sex marriage on 9 June 2015 and said he would formulate a bill to repeal the island's marriage prohibition, a commitment that preceded the 2016 Act.

The criminal-law record runs from decriminalisation of private consensual acts between men in September 1992, when the age of consent was set at twenty-one, through the Criminal Justice Act 2001 (c.4), which lowered it to eighteen, to the Sexual Offences (Amendment) Act 2006 (c.3), which lowered it to sixteen and made the law gender-neutral for all sexual conduct regardless of gender and sexual orientation. Until 2021, Section 9 of the Sexual Offences Act 1992 retained offences of buggery and gross indecency between men where a participant was under sixteen or the act was committed other than in private, with Section 10 defining other than in private as more than two people present or a place to which the public had access. The Sexual Offences and Obscene Publications Act 2021 deleted the more-than-two-people specification and made the language on indecent exposure and sexual activity in a public place gender-neutral.

The Sexual Offences and Obscene Publications Act 2021 received royal assent in July 2021 and took effect on 1 July 2022 by proclamation. It pardoned historical convictions for gay sex offences committed before 1992, following the United Kingdom's 2017 Turing law. Chief Minister Howard Quayle issued an unqualified apology to men convicted under the earlier laws, and in August 2022, on the thirtieth anniversary of decriminalisation, the police commissioner formally apologised for enforcement of anti-gay laws up to 1992.
localsOnly:
Employment protection began with an amendment to the Employment Bill adopted by the House of Keys on 30 November 2005 and tabled by Onchan MHK Peter Karran, which barred dismissal of gay and lesbian employees on sexual-orientation grounds and aligned the island with United Kingdom human-rights law. The Employment Act 2006 (c.21) took effect on 1 September 2006. The Equality Act 2017 lists sexual orientation, defined to include attraction to the same sex, the opposite sex or either sex as well as lack of attraction to either sex, as a protected characteristic alongside gender reassignment.

The island's only functioning prison is at Jurby, a GBP 41.7m facility on the site of the former RAF Jurby that became fully operational on 14 August 2008 and is run by the Isle of Man Prison Service. It has separate units for remand and convicted prisoners, for female prisoners, for young offenders and for vulnerable prisoners, plus a segregation unit. No rule on placement by birth sex against gender identity, no trans-specific unit and no trans-specific segregation practice are documented.
outOfScopeNotes:
No rule on identity-document markers for trans residents or visitors is documented in the sources reviewed, and no entry, visa or border-screening procedure is recorded that would require disclosure of a trans visitor's status.

Whether the legal gender recognition process under the Gender Recognition Act 2009 is open to people who are not resident on the island is not established by the sources reviewed.

Hate-crime protection covering gender identity rests on a July 2022 consultation proposal; the sources reviewed do not show an enacted provision, or how such a provision would be enforced.

No trans-specific violence figures, prosecutions or documented incidents on the island appear in the sources reviewed.
